1-1.title: Describing and Classifying Matter
1-1.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space (volume). You, the air, a desk, and a drop of water are all matter.

Scientists describe matter by its properties:
- Physical properties can be observed WITHOUT changing what the substance is — color, hardness, texture, melting point, boiling point, density.
- Chemical properties describe how matter REACTS to form new substances — flammability (burning), or the ability to rust.

Example 1 — Physical vs. chemical property
The color of gold and the fact that ice melts at 0°C are physical properties (no new substance forms). The fact that iron can rust or paper can burn are chemical properties (a NEW substance forms).

Example 2 — Pure substance vs. mixture
A pure substance is made of only one kind of matter (like pure water or pure copper). A mixture is two or more substances physically combined but NOT chemically joined (like salad, or salt water). In a mixture you can often separate the parts again.

Example 3 — Classify
Sugar dissolved in tea = a mixture. A bar of pure silver = a pure substance. Air = a mixture of gases.

questions.question: Which statement best defines matter?

choices.A: Anything that has mass and takes up space
choices.C: Only solid objects you can hold

questions.explanation: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space (volume), including solids, liquids, and gases.

questions.question: Which of these is a physical property of a substance?
questions.explanation: Color can be observed without changing the substance, so it is a physical property. Rusting, burning, and reacting with acid form new substances, so they are chemical properties.

questions.question: Which is an example of a chemical property?

questions.question: Which list contains ONLY physical properties?

questions.question: Which BEST explains the difference between a pure substance and a mixture?

choices.C: how the object reacts with acid
choices.D: how much space an object takes up

questions.question: Which of these is NOT matter?

questions.question: Texture, like whether a rock is rough or smooth, is an example of a
questions.explanation: Texture can be observed without changing the substance, so it is a physical property.

questions.question: Which of these is a pure substance?
questions.explanation: Pure copper is made of only one kind of matter, so it is a pure substance. Salad, salt water, and air are mixtures.

questions.question: A key feature of a mixture is that

choices.A: the parts are chemically joined and cannot be separated
choices.B: the parts can often be separated again
choices.C: it is always made of only one substance
choices.D: it always forms a new substance

questions.explanation: In a mixture the substances are only physically combined, so the parts can often be separated again.

questions.question: Which property tells you how matter REACTS to form a new substance?
questions.explanation: A chemical property describes how matter reacts to form a new substance, such as flammability or the ability to rust.

questions.question: Sugar dissolved in tea is best classified as a
questions.explanation: Sugar and tea are physically combined but not chemically joined, so the result is a mixture.

questions.question: Which of the following is a chemical property of iron?

choices.B: It is a solid at room temperature
choices.C: It can rust when exposed to air and water
choices.D: It can be bent into shapes

questions.explanation: Rusting forms a new substance, so the ability to rust is a chemical property. Color, state, and bendability are physical properties.

choices.C: The silver is a pure substance and the salt water is a mixture

questions.explanation: Pure silver is one kind of matter (a pure substance), while salt water is two substances combined (a mixture).

questions.question: Which of these can be observed WITHOUT changing what the substance is?
questions.explanation: Melting point is a physical property that can be measured without changing the substance. Burning, rusting, and reacting with acid are chemical properties.

questions.question: A chef notices that a wooden match can catch fire. The ability to catch fire is called
questions.explanation: Flammability is the ability to burn and form new substances, which is a chemical property.

questions.question: Which list contains ONLY chemical properties?

choices.B: Flammability, ability to rust, reactivity with acid

questions.explanation: Flammability, the ability to rust, and reactivity with acid all describe forming new substances, so all three are chemical properties.

questions.question: Hardness, such as how easily a mineral is scratched, is which type of property?
questions.explanation: Hardness can be observed without changing the substance, so it is a physical property.

questions.question: Which is the BEST example of a pure substance?
questions.explanation: Distilled water is made of only one kind of matter, so it is a pure substance. The others are mixtures.

questions.question: Why is being able to separate the parts a clue that something is a mixture?

choices.A: Because the substances are chemically joined
choices.C: Because a new substance has formed
choices.D: Because the substances are only physically combined, not chemically joined

questions.explanation: In a mixture the substances are only physically combined, so they can be separated again.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a physical property?
questions.explanation: The ability to burn forms a new substance, so it is a chemical property, not a physical property.

questions.question: A student says, 'I can describe this gold ring by its color and shine without changing it.' These are
questions.explanation: Color and shine (luster) are observed without changing the substance, so they are physical properties.

questions.question: Lemonade made from water, lemon juice, and sugar is an example of a
questions.explanation: Lemonade is several substances physically combined but not chemically joined, so it is a mixture.

questions.question: Which BEST compares physical and chemical properties?

choices.B: Physical properties can be observed without changing the substance; chemical properties describe forming new substances
choices.C: Chemical properties never involve new substances

questions.explanation: Physical properties are observed without changing the substance, while chemical properties describe how matter reacts to form new substances.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of matter?
questions.explanation: A glass of milk has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Heat, sound, and shadows are not matter.

questions.question: A scientist tests whether a metal reacts with acid to bubble and form a new substance. This test measures a

questions.question: Which statement about a mixture is FALSE?

choices.A: It contains two or more substances
choices.C: Its substances are chemically joined into one new substance

questions.explanation: In a mixture the substances are NOT chemically joined into a new substance; they are only physically combined.

questions.explanation: Ocean water is several substances physically combined but not chemically joined, so it is a mixture.

questions.question: Which of these BEST shows a chemical property in action?

choices.C: Old silver tarnishes and turns dark when it reacts with air

questions.explanation: Tarnishing forms a new substance on the silver, so it shows a chemical property. Bending, feeling cold, and being heavy are physical.

questions.question: Trail mix containing peanuts, raisins, and chocolate pieces is a mixture because

choices.A: the parts are chemically joined into a new food
choices.B: the parts are physically combined and could be picked apart

questions.question: Which property would help you identify a substance WITHOUT changing it into something new?

questions.question: A teacher shows that pure copper is always made of the same one kind of matter. This makes copper a

questions.question: Which is the BEST reason color is called a physical property?

choices.A: Color changes the substance into a new one

choices.C: Color tells how the substance reacts with acid

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a mixture?
questions.explanation: Pure oxygen gas is one kind of matter, so it is a pure substance, not a mixture. The others are mixtures.

questions.question: A student must sort items as 'pure substance' or 'mixture.' Which item belongs in the 'pure substance' group?

choices.A: A cup of coffee with cream
choices.C: A bowl of cereal with milk

1-2.title: Measuring Matter
1-2.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Scientists measure matter in three main ways:
- Mass = how much matter an object contains. Measured in grams (g) with a balance.
- Volume = how much space an object takes up. Measured in milliliters (mL) or cubic centimeters (cm³).
- Density = how tightly matter is packed = mass divided by volume (D = m ÷ V).

Example 1 — Calculate density
A rock has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 20 mL.
Density = mass ÷ volume = 60 g ÷ 20 mL = 3 g/mL.

Example 2 — Same size, different density
A beach ball and a small steel ball can be very different sizes, but density depends on BOTH mass and volume. A small steel ball sinks because it has high density; a large beach ball floats because its density is low (lots of volume, little mass).

Example 3 — Float or sink?
Objects with a density LESS than water (1 g/mL) float; objects with a density GREATER than water sink. A 3 g/mL rock sinks; a 0.9 g/mL piece of ice floats.

choices.A: how much space an object takes up
choices.B: how much matter an object contains

questions.explanation: Mass measures how much matter an object contains and is measured in grams.

questions.question: Which unit is commonly used to measure volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is measured in milliliters (mL) or cubic centimeters (cm³).

questions.question: Density is calculated by
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume. It tells how tightly matter is packed.

questions.question: A block has a mass of 40 g and a volume of 8 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density = 40 g ÷ 8 cm³ = 5 g/cm³.

questions.explanation: Objects with a density less than water (1 g/mL) float, so a 0.8 g/mL object floats.

questions.question: A liquid has a mass of 50 g and a volume of 50 mL. Its density is
questions.explanation: Density = 50 g ÷ 50 mL = 1 g/mL.

questions.question: Why can a small steel ball sink while a much larger beach ball floats?

choices.B: Density depends on both mass and volume, and steel is much denser than the beach ball
choices.C: The beach ball has more mass

questions.explanation: Density depends on mass AND volume. Steel packs much more mass into a small volume, so it is denser and sinks.

questions.question: Which tool would a scientist use to measure the mass of a rock?
questions.explanation: A balance measures mass. Thermometers measure temperature, rulers measure length, and stopwatches measure time.

questions.question: Two cubes are the same size, but Cube A has more mass than Cube B. Which is true?

choices.A: Cube A has a higher density
choices.B: Cube B has a higher density

questions.explanation: With equal volume, the cube with more mass has the higher density (D = m ÷ V).

choices.B: 1 g/cm³; it neither clearly sinks nor floats

questions.explanation: Density = 27 ÷ 27 = 1 g/cm³, the same as water, so it neither clearly sinks nor floats.

questions.question: Which unit is used to measure mass?
questions.explanation: Mass is measured in grams using a balance.

questions.question: A rock has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 20 mL. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density = 60 g ÷ 20 mL = 3 g/mL.

questions.question: Density measures
questions.explanation: Density tells how tightly matter is packed and equals mass divided by volume.

questions.explanation: An object denser than water (greater than 1 g/mL) sinks.

questions.question: Which tool measures the volume of a liquid?
questions.explanation: A graduated cylinder measures the volume of a liquid in milliliters.

questions.question: A piece of ice has a density of about 0.9 g/mL. In a glass of water it will

questions.question: A cube has a mass of 100 g and a volume of 25 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density = 100 g ÷ 25 cm³ = 4 g/cm³.

questions.question: Which is the correct formula for density?
questions.explanation: Density is found by dividing mass by volume (D = m ÷ V).

questions.question: Two balls are the same size, but the steel ball has much more mass than the foam ball. Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: With equal volume, the ball with more mass (steel) has the higher density.

questions.question: Why does a large beach ball float while a small steel ball sinks?

choices.A: Because the beach ball has more mass
choices.B: Because the steel ball is larger
choices.C: Because the beach ball has low density (much volume, little mass) and steel has high density

questions.explanation: Density depends on both mass and volume. The beach ball has a lot of volume but little mass (low density), while steel packs much mass into a small volume (high density).

questions.question: A liquid has a mass of 30 g and a volume of 10 mL. Its density is
questions.explanation: Density = 30 g ÷ 10 mL = 3 g/mL.

questions.question: Which measurement would you use to find out how much space a box takes up?
questions.explanation: Volume measures how much space an object takes up.

questions.question: A scientist needs to measure how much matter is in a sample. Which property should be measured?
questions.explanation: Mass measures how much matter an object contains.

questions.question: An object's density is exactly equal to water's density of 1 g/mL. The object will MOST likely

choices.B: shoot up out of the water
choices.C: neither clearly sink nor clearly float

questions.explanation: An object with the same density as water neither clearly sinks nor clearly floats.

questions.question: A 50 cm³ block of wood has a mass of 25 g. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density = 25 g ÷ 50 cm³ = 0.5 g/cm³.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a way scientists measure matter?
questions.explanation: Mass, volume, and density are ways to measure matter. Loudness measures sound, not matter.

questions.question: A wooden block (density 0.6 g/cm³) is placed in water (density 1 g/cm³). What happens?

choices.A: It sinks because it is solid
choices.B: It floats because its density is less than water's
choices.D: It sinks because wood is heavy

questions.explanation: The block's density (0.6 g/cm³) is less than water's (1 g/cm³), so it floats.

questions.question: Which BEST explains why density is useful for identifying a substance?

choices.A: Density changes every time you cut the object
choices.D: Density is the same for a given substance no matter the size of the sample

questions.explanation: A given substance has the same density no matter how big the sample is, so density helps identify it.

questions.question: A balance reads 45 g for a sample, and a graduated cylinder shows its volume is 15 mL. What is the density?
questions.explanation: Density = 45 g ÷ 15 mL = 3 g/mL.

questions.question: Volume can be measured in
questions.explanation: Volume is measured in milliliters (mL) or cubic centimeters (cm³).

questions.question: A student wants to find a rock's volume. The rock has an odd shape. The BEST method is to

choices.C: time how long it takes to fall
choices.D: drop it in water and measure how much the water level rises

questions.explanation: An irregular object's volume can be found by water displacement: the rise in water level equals the object's volume.

questions.question: Which object has the GREATEST density: 10 g in 2 mL, 10 g in 5 mL, or 10 g in 10 mL?
questions.explanation: With the same mass, the smallest volume gives the highest density: 10 g ÷ 2 mL = 5 g/mL, the largest value.

questions.question: A sample of oil has a density of 0.92 g/mL. If oil and water are poured together, the oil will

choices.B: float on top of the water

questions.explanation: Oil is less dense than water (0.92 g/mL is less than 1 g/mL), so the oil floats on top.

questions.question: What does a balance measure?
questions.explanation: A balance measures mass, the amount of matter in an object.

questions.question: A 200 g object has a volume of 100 cm³. What is its density, and will it float in water?
questions.explanation: Density = 200 g ÷ 100 cm³ = 2 g/cm³. Since 2 g/cm³ is greater than water's 1 g/cm³, the object sinks.

questions.question: Which statement about mass and volume is correct?

choices.A: Mass is space and volume is matter
choices.B: Mass and volume are the same thing
choices.D: Mass is the amount of matter and volume is the space it takes up

questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter an object contains, and volume is how much space it takes up.

questions.question: A golden ring has a mass of 38.6 g and a volume of 2 cm³. Its density is about
questions.explanation: Density = 38.6 g ÷ 2 cm³ = 19.3 g/cm³.

questions.question: Two objects have the same mass, but Object X has a larger volume than Object Y. Which has the lower density?
questions.explanation: With equal mass, the object with the larger volume has the lower density (D = m ÷ V).

questions.question: Which measurement does NOT change if you move an object from Earth to the Moon?
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and does not change with location.

questions.question: A student measures a marble's mass as 12 g and its volume as 4 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density = 12 g ÷ 4 cm³ = 3 g/cm³.

1-3.title: Changes in Matter
1-3.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Matter changes in two main ways:
- A physical change alters how matter LOOKS but keeps it the SAME substance. Examples: ice melting into water, tearing paper, dissolving sugar, bending a wire. Physical changes are often easy to reverse.
- A chemical change turns matter into a BRAND-NEW substance. Examples: wood burning into ash, iron rusting, food cooking, milk souring.

Signs of a chemical change: a color change, bubbles or gas forming, light or heat given off, a new smell, or a change you can't easily undo.

Example 1 — Melting ice
Ice melting to water is a PHYSICAL change. It is still water (H₂O); only the state changed. You can refreeze it.

Example 2 — Burning wood
Burning wood is a CHEMICAL change. The wood turns into ash, smoke, and gases — new substances you cannot turn back into wood.

Example 3 — Bubbles and color
When vinegar and baking soda fizz, the bubbles (gas) signal a chemical change. When iron turns reddish-brown (rust), the color change signals a chemical change.

questions.question: Which is an example of a physical change?
questions.explanation: Ice melting keeps the same substance (water); only the state changes, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which is an example of a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Burning paper creates new substances (ash, smoke, gases), so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: Which is a clue that a chemical change has happened?

choices.B: Bubbles of a new gas form
choices.D: The object was cut in half

questions.explanation: Forming bubbles of a new gas is a sign of a chemical change. Changing shape, getting wet, or cutting are physical changes.

questions.question: In a physical change, the substance
questions.explanation: In a physical change, the matter stays the same substance even though it may look different.

questions.question: Dissolving sugar in water is considered a physical change because

choices.B: the sugar is still sugar and could be recovered

questions.explanation: The sugar stays sugar (no new substance) and could be recovered by evaporating the water, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of a chemical change?

choices.D: Water changing shape to fit a cup

questions.explanation: Water taking the shape of its container is a physical change. Color change, heat/light, and new smells are signs of chemical change.

questions.question: When iron rusts, it turns reddish-brown. This is a chemical change because
questions.explanation: Rust is a new substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen, so rusting is a chemical change.

questions.question: Which change could MOST easily be reversed?
questions.explanation: Freezing water is a physical change that can be reversed by melting. Burning, cooking, and rusting are chemical changes that are hard to reverse.

questions.question: A student crushes a piece of chalk into powder. What kind of change is this?

choices.A: A chemical change, because new substances form
choices.B: A physical change, because it is still chalk
choices.C: A chemical change, because the color changed

questions.explanation: Crushing chalk only changes its size and shape; it is still chalk, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Cooking pancake batter on a hot griddle is a chemical change MAINLY because

choices.A: the batter changes into new substances that cannot easily turn back

questions.explanation: Cooking turns the batter into new substances (the cooked pancake) that cannot easily be turned back, so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: In a chemical change, matter
questions.explanation: A chemical change turns matter into a brand-new substance.

questions.question: Which is an example of a physical change?
questions.explanation: Tearing paper changes its shape but it is still paper, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which is a sign that a chemical change has happened?

choices.C: The object got colder by sitting outside
choices.D: The object was cut into pieces

questions.explanation: A new smell appearing is a sign of a chemical change. Changing shape, getting cold by sitting, or cutting are physical changes.

questions.question: Melting an ice cube into water is a physical change because

choices.A: the water becomes a new substance
choices.C: the water turns into a gas forever
choices.D: it is still water (H₂O) and can be refrozen

questions.explanation: Melted ice is still water and can be refrozen, so only the state changed; it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a sign of a chemical change?

choices.A: Bubbles of a new gas forming
choices.B: Light or heat being given off
choices.D: An ice cube melting into water

questions.explanation: An ice cube melting is a physical change. Bubbles of new gas, light or heat, and color changes are signs of chemical change.

questions.question: Burning wood is a chemical change because

choices.B: the wood gets a little wet
choices.C: the wood is cut into smaller pieces
choices.D: the wood turns into ash, smoke, and gases that cannot turn back into wood

questions.explanation: Burning wood forms new substances (ash, smoke, and gases) that cannot be turned back into wood, so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: When vinegar and baking soda are mixed, they fizz and bubble. This fizzing is a sign of

choices.A: a chemical change, because a new gas forms

questions.explanation: The bubbles are a new gas forming, which is a sign of a chemical change.

questions.question: Bending a metal wire into a new shape is
questions.explanation: Bending a wire changes its shape but it is still the same metal, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which change would be the HARDEST to reverse?
questions.explanation: Burning toast is a chemical change that forms new substances and is very hard to reverse. The others are physical changes.

questions.question: Which BEST describes a physical change?

choices.A: Matter changes how it looks but stays the same substance
choices.B: Matter turns into a brand-new substance

questions.explanation: In a physical change, matter changes how it looks but stays the same substance.

questions.question: Souring milk is a chemical change because

choices.B: the milk changes shape in the glass
choices.C: the milk turns into new substances with a new smell and taste

questions.explanation: Souring milk forms new substances, shown by the new smell and taste, so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: Which list shows ONLY physical changes?

choices.A: Melting ice, tearing paper, bending a wire
choices.B: Burning wood, rusting iron, cooking an egg
choices.C: Melting ice, burning wood, souring milk
choices.D: Tearing paper, rusting iron, cooking food

questions.explanation: Melting ice, tearing paper, and bending a wire all keep the same substance, so all three are physical changes.

questions.question: A student dissolves salt in water. This is a physical change because

choices.D: the salt is still salt and could be recovered by evaporating the water

questions.explanation: The salt stays salt and could be recovered by evaporating the water, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which observation is the BEST evidence of a chemical change?

choices.A: A liquid is poured into a different cup
choices.B: A solid is broken into smaller pieces
choices.C: A burning candle gives off light and heat and forms new gases

questions.explanation: A burning candle gives off light and heat and forms new gases, which are signs of a chemical change.

questions.question: Chopping a carrot into slices is

choices.A: a chemical change, because new substances form
choices.B: a physical change, because it is still carrot
choices.C: a chemical change, because the color changes

questions.explanation: Chopping only changes the carrot's size and shape; it is still carrot, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which change can MOST easily be undone?

choices.B: Melting chocolate, then cooling it back into a solid

questions.explanation: Melting chocolate and cooling it again is a physical change that can be reversed. The others are chemical changes that are hard to undo.

questions.question: A nail left outside slowly turns reddish-brown. This change is

choices.A: physical, because the nail kept its shape
choices.B: chemical, because rust is a new substance
choices.C: physical, because the nail only got wet

questions.explanation: Rust is a new substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen, so this is a chemical change.

questions.question: Which of these is a physical change?
questions.explanation: Crushing a can changes its shape but it is still the same metal, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Why is boiling water into steam a physical change?

choices.A: The steam is a new substance, not water
choices.B: The water reacts with the air to form a new gas
choices.D: The steam is still water (H₂O) and can cool back into liquid water

questions.explanation: Steam is still water that can cool back into liquid, so boiling is a physical change of state.

questions.question: Which is an example of a chemical change?

choices.B: An apple slice turning brown after sitting out
choices.D: Pouring apple juice into a cup

questions.explanation: An apple slice turning brown happens because it reacts with air to form a new substance, so it is a chemical change.

questions.question: A campfire gives off heat and light and leaves behind ash. This shows that burning is a
questions.explanation: Heat, light, and ash (a new substance) are signs of a chemical change.

questions.question: Which statement about physical changes is TRUE?

choices.A: They always create a new substance
choices.B: They are often easy to reverse

questions.explanation: Physical changes keep the same substance and are often easy to reverse, like melting and refreezing.

questions.question: Which change is DIFFERENT from the others?
questions.explanation: Paper burning is a chemical change that forms new substances. The others are physical changes that keep the same substance.

questions.question: Toasting bread until it turns brown and gives off a new smell is a chemical change because

choices.C: new substances formed, shown by the color and smell change

questions.explanation: The color change and new smell show that new substances formed, so toasting is a chemical change.

questions.question: A student folds a paper airplane. This is best described as a
questions.explanation: Folding paper changes its shape but it is still paper, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Water freezing into ice is a physical change; it is still water. Rusting, burning, and baking form new substances.

questions.question: During a science lab, a clear liquid is added to another and the mixture suddenly turns bright blue. The color change is a sign of
questions.explanation: A color change that signals a new substance is a sign of a chemical change.

questions.question: Which BEST explains the difference between a physical and a chemical change?

choices.A: A physical change makes a new substance; a chemical change does not
choices.B: Both changes always make new substances
choices.C: Neither change can ever be reversed
choices.D: A physical change keeps the same substance; a chemical change makes a new substance

questions.explanation: A physical change keeps the same substance, while a chemical change makes a brand-new substance.

questions.question: A glass of water is left in the freezer and turns to ice. This change is physical because

choices.A: the water became a new substance
choices.D: the ice can melt back into the same water

questions.explanation: The ice can melt back into the same water, showing only the state changed, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Which set of clues TOGETHER best suggests a chemical change took place?

choices.A: The object changed shape and got wet
choices.B: The object was cut and then folded
choices.C: Gas bubbles formed, the color changed, and heat was given off
choices.D: The object was poured into a new container

questions.explanation: Gas forming, a color change, and heat being given off are all signs of a chemical change, so together they strongly suggest one occurred.
